title: SAO Breakdown: When GRPO’s Group Sampling Collides with Asynchronous Agent Training, How to Rescue After Collapse at Step 160
subtitle: Single-Rollout Asynchronous Optimization: Bringing Back the Value Model Deleted by GRPO
markdown: > Breakdown Target: Single-Rollout Asynchronous Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning (arXiv:2607.07508, submitted 2026-07-08), currently a preprint, not yet formally accepted by top conferences (dblp only lists it as CoRR abs/2607.07508). Authors: Zhenyu Hou, Yujiang Li (equal contribution, completed during internship at Z.AI), Jie Tang, Yuxiao Dong, from the KEG Lab at Tsinghua University. SAO has been deployed in the agentic RL training pipeline of the open-source model GLM-5.2 (750B-A40B). This breakdown does one thing: analyze why its structure is good. All numbers and formulas come from the arXiv v1 main text and appendix, which can be cross-checked against the original tables. ## 1. Why It’s Worth Breaking Down The rollout lengths for long-horizon Agent tasks vary drastically: one encoding trajectory might run for 128k tokens, while another ends in just a few steps. Synchronous RL pipelines must wait for the entire batch of rollouts to finish before updating, leaving GPUs idle for large periods. Thus, asynchronous RL (training immediately as soon as a rollout arrives) becomes an efficiency necessity. The problem lies on the algorithmic side. GRPO’s group sampling requires generating a group of rollouts for the same prompt, using the group mean as the baseline. In an asynchronous setting, a group must wait for the slowest long trajectory; during this waiting period, the policy has already been updated, destroying the "simultaneity" of the group samples. This waiting itself introduces off-policy bias. The paper’s empirical results are harsh: **vanilla GRPO collapses in performance after about 160 steps in an asynchronous setting (Figure 3)**. SAO’s answer is to replace GRPO’s sampling primitive entirely: generate only one rollout per prompt, and train upon completion. Since a single rollout has no group baseline available, we bring back the value model that GRPO had deleted. The value of this paper lies in its systematic answer to "what maintains training stability after removing group sampling," and it has already been validated on a 750B production pipeline. It forms a perfect contrastive reading with DAPO: DAPO fixes four failure modes of GRPO in synchronous settings, while SAO points out structural failures of GRPO in asynchronous settings. Both fixes operate at the level of token-level importance handling. ## 2. Main Text Skeleton: The method occupies only one section, but experiments take up four and a half sections | Section | Responsibility | Key Breakdown Points | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 Introduction | Establish Argument | Synchronous pipelines are inefficient for long-horizon tasks + existing asynchronous systems focus on throughput while ignoring stability; dual motivations presented side-by-side | | 2 Preliminaries | Preliminaries | Formalizes off-policy asynchronous RL, paving the way for DIS and single rollout | | 3 Asynchronous RL with Single Rollout | Main Method | 3.1 DIS stabilizes asynchronous training; 3.2 single rollout reduces off-policy bias. The two subsections are ordered as "stabilize first, then generalize" | | 4 Experiments | Main Experiments | 4.2 Main results, 4.3 Ablation studies, 4.4 Training dynamics, 4.5 Online learning simulation. The four subsections progress layer by layer | | 5 Related Work | Related Work | Placed in Section 5 rather than Section 2 to avoid interrupting the "problem, method, evidence" narrative thread | | 6 Conclusion + Appendix A/B | Conclusion | Appendix A contains suboptimal baselines at the step-level action granularity; Appendix B honestly discusses limitations | Notable ordering detail: Related work is placed in Section 5. Most papers habitually place it in Section 2. This paper's method narrative follows a clear causal chain (synchronous inefficiency → asynchronous → asynchronous disrupts grouped sampling → switch sampling primitive → introduce new problems → solve them one by one). Placing related work upfront would interrupt this chain. ## III. Four Mechanisms: One Primitive Replacement, Three Supporting Engineering Solutions Section 3 and the experimental design present four mechanisms, arranged in dependency order according to "replace primitive, supplement baseline, prevent noise, prevent divergence": | Mechanism | Target Object | Key Design | | --- | --- | --- | | Single rollout sampling | Sampling primitive | Each prompt generates only one trajectory; training proceeds immediately upon completion, eliminating group waiting (Figure 2 overview) | | Value model reinforcement | Baseline estimation | Critic update frequency is twice that of the Actor; freeze the attention parameters of the value model, training only the MoE projection layer; expand the value pre-training corpus to address cold-start issues | | Token-level GAE skipping observations | Value propagation over multi-step trajectories | Advantages propagate only between action tokens, directly linking to the next action across environment observation intervals (Equations 4 and 5) | | DIS bilateral clipping | importance sampling | directly calculates the ratio using log probabilities recorded by the rollout engine, completely discarding π_old; tokens falling outside `[1-ε_low, 1+ε_high]` are entirely masked from the gradient | The three supporting designs each have clear fault attribution, which is the most valuable part of the entire article to learn from: 1. **Why the critic update is twice as fast**: The gradient estimation variance of a single rollout is naturally higher than that of a group-mean baseline; the value model must learn faster than the policy to suppress variance. Policy learning rate 1×10⁻⁶, value model 5×10⁻⁶ 2. **Why freeze attention**: The authors empirically found that the instability of the value model mainly comes from the Full Attention layer, whose gradient norm is significantly larger than that of the policy model; MoE layers are relatively stable. Freezing attention only trains the MoE projection layer, achieving a win-win for memory and stability. The implicit assumption is that the pre-trained attention weights already possess sufficient semantic capability. 3. **Why skip observation tokens**: Multi-turn trajectory T = [a₀, o₀, a₁, o₁, …], where environmental feedback oᵢ is not generated by the model. The value model is forced to predict the "value of the external environmental state," which only injects noise. The TD residual in Equation 5 directly skips the observation interval, connecting the value of action i to action i+1. The hyperparameters of DIS are worth noting separately: mathematical reasoning takes `ε_low = 0.3, ε_high = 5.0`, coding Agent takes `ε_low = 0.8, ε_high = 3.0`. The upper and lower bounds are severely asymmetric, and the upper bound can be increased to 5.0, because the goal is the mild action of "masking extreme outlier tokens," so the clipping interval can be much more aggressive than PPO. It is interesting to read this in comparison with DAPO's Clip-Higher: both use asymmetric intervals, but DAPO uses it to increase entropy, while SAO uses it to prevent divergence. ## 4. Main Results and Ablation: Dissecting the Contribution of Each Mechanism The main results are presented in two tables: Table 1 for mathematical reasoning (AIME2025 / BeyondAIME / HMMT / IMOAnswerBench), Table 2 for coding (SWE-Bench Verified). The base model is Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507: | Benchmark | Baseline | GRPO (w/ DIS) | SAO | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | SWE-Bench Verified | 23.0 | 27.0 | **29.8** | | AIME 2025 (Python tool) | 80.4 | 84.2 | **97.3** | | BeyondAIME | 53.3 | 54.8 | **74.8** | | HMMT | - | 76.0 | **88.3** | | IMOAnswerBench | - | 55.8 | **74.0** | In the control group, GPT-5 High scores 94.6 / 74.0 / 89.2 / 76.0 across the four mathematical benchmarks. SAO surpasses on two items and is close on two others with the 30B base. The information content of this comparison table is greater than the absolute scores. The ablation section (Tables 3 and 4) is similarly organized by "how much score drops when which mechanism is removed": | Configuration | AIME 2025 | BeyondAIME | | --- | --- | --- | | Full SAO | 97.3 | 74.8 | | Remove critic double update | 95.0 | 69.8 | | Remove attention freezing | 90.6 | 74.5 | | Vanilla VAPO (w/o DIS) | 91.3 | 69.0 (rapid training collapse) | | Running-mean baseline replacing value model | 79.8 | 55.3 | This table firmly establishes the necessity of "value model regression": replacing it with a running-mean baseline causes a direct drop of 17.5 points, which is larger than the loss from any single engineering trick. Figure 4's training dynamics analysis (explained variance, critic gradient norm, clipping ratio) explains why: the VAPO baseline collapses around step 90, and DIS is a prerequisite for asynchronous training to proceed. A point to read with caution: ablations are only performed on the 30B base model, while the GLM-5.2 750B deployment represents a single-point production validation without controlled A/B testing, and the paper provides no information on the compute cost of that training. The scale jump between "ablations on 30B" and "deployment on 750B" is currently bridged by trust. ## V. GLM-5.2 Deployment: A One-Sentence Production Endorsement, and Honest Boundaries The paper's entire discussion of GLM-5.2 deployment is limited to one sentence in the abstract: SAO has been deployed in the agentic RL training pipeline for GLM-5.2 (750B-A40B). The main text provides no deployment details, no evaluation metrics, and no hardware configurations. Appendix B, conversely, clarifies the deployment prerequisites: SAO relies on a pre-trained value model and token-level rollout log probabilities, requiring infrastructure capable of reliably retaining these probabilities during asynchronous generation processes. This writing style of "providing an endorsement without replication details" is a double-edged sword: for paper credibility, the adoption of flagship models in production serves as the strongest proof of existence; for readers attempting replication, engineering details at the pipeline level must be sought within Z.AI's slime framework (the GLM series' RL training infrastructure, which is open source). The paper itself does not provide an open code repository, which stands in sharp contrast to DAPO's fully open-source approach (code, data, and weights), thereby defining the reproducibility boundaries of both papers. ## VI. Three Writing Techniques Worth Learning 1. **Pin down the opponent's failure mode before establishing your argument**: The "GRPO 160-step collapse" curve in Figure 3 is placed before the main experiments. Readers enter the methods section with the empirical impression that "it indeed collapses," making the argument for the necessity of each mechanism easier. 2. **Design ablation tables as "death certificates for mechanisms"**: The row for the running-mean baseline scoring 79.8 stands alone to prove that "removing the value model is a dead end." This is a harsher writing style than positive accumulation. 3. **Place the limitations section in the main text appendix rather than hiding it in the discussion**: Appendix B explicitly lists three boundaries: value model overhead, infrastructure dependencies, and single-lab results. The sense of honesty in engineering papers comes from proactively disclosing applicable conditions. ## Endnote: Genealogical Position and Mapping to My Own Work Placed within the training genealogy of GRPO, SAO represents a directional turning point: GRPO (2024) started by removing the value model, DAPO (March 2025) fixed its synchronization faults, GSPO (July 2025) stabilized its MoE training, and SAO (July 2026) brought the value model back in asynchronous scenarios. The criterion for algorithmic evolution remains the task morphology: short-range verifiable tasks are sufficient with the GRPO series, while long-range asynchronous Agent tasks require token-level credit allocation, making the cost of this critic unavoidable. For the AI post-match coaching system I am working on, the direct inspiration lies in the design of "GAE skipping observation": the trajectory understanding of post-match coaches also faces multi-turn sequences where "model outputs" and "environment feedback" (game logs, telemetry data) alternate. When performing value propagation or attribution on environment feedback segments, the problem of noise injection is isomorphic. When the algorithm layer outputs structured JSON evidence, explicitly partitioning "model-interpretable actions" and "environment-given states" within the token sequence is an engineering version of the same design philosophy. ## References - Paper: arXiv:2607.07508 (2026-07-08), Zhenyu Hou, Yujiang Li, Jie Tang, Yuxiao Dong, Tsinghua University KEG - Production Deployment: GLM-5.2 (750B-A40B, MIT open source) agentic RL pipeline; infrastructure corresponds to Z.AI's open-source slime framework - Main Experiment Protocol: Base Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507, batch size 128, max length 128k tokens, SWE-Bench Verified using OpenHands scaffold (max 300 interaction rounds); math benchmark reports mean of 16 runs (BeyondAIME is 4 runs), top-p = 1.0, temperature = 1.0 - Comparative reading: DAPO (arXiv:2503.14476), our breakdown can be found in "DAPO Breakdown: How Four Mechanisms Boost GRPO's Score on AIME 2024 from 30 to 50"
